rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Temperature is a measure of AVERAGE kinetic energy, not the kinetic energy of any single molecule. A hot object has higher average KE per molecule, but individual molecules have a range of speeds.  ·  The kinetic theory assumes perfectly elastic collisions. In reality, some kinetic energy is lost to internal excitation (vibration, rotation) or radiation, especially in gases with complex molecules.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Temperature can be defined for any system in thermal equilibrium, but the kinetic energy definition $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$ applies specifically to translational kinetic energy in ideal gases. Rotational and vibrational energy also contribute to temperature.  ·  The mean free path is inversely proportional to number density (n) and collision cross-section (σ). At higher pressure (lower volume), molecules are closer together and collide more frequently, reducing the mean free path.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The kinetic theory was first proposed by Daniel Bernoulli in 1738 in his work 'Hydrodynamica', but it was largely ignored until revived by Clausius, Maxwell, and Boltzmann in the 19th century.  ·  Maxwell and Boltzmann independently developed the distribution of molecular speeds in the 1860s-1870s. The distribution is now called the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.

rows.text: **Postulates (Four fundamental assumptions):**  ·  1. A gas consists of a large number of identical, point-like molecules with negligible volume (point particles).  ·  2. The molecules are in constant, random motion. No two molecules occupy the same point in space.
